Gastroenterology · published research

Anal sphincter injury

Two rabbit experiments reported improved sphincter pressure or tissue-repair measures after PBM, with some outcomes strongest in combination groups. No human study was identified.

PBM Database summary

What the records report

Two rabbit experiments reported improved sphincter pressure or tissue-repair measures after PBM, with some outcomes strongest in combination groups. No human study was identified.

Summary of the Evidence

Two publications report five-arm experiments in male rabbits after surgical anal sphincter injury, each with 35 animals and 90-day follow-up. They came from the same Iranian research group but tested different combinations: human adipose-derived stem cells in 2019 and chondroitinase ABC in 2021. The papers describe separate experiments; no cohort duplication is indicated, although the shared model and team mean they are not independent replications by different investigators. Neither study tested patients.

Human and clinical evidence

No human clinical study of PBM for anal sphincter injury was identified in the indication records. The animal outcome of sphincter pressure is relevant to continence, but it does not show that PBM restores continence or prevents symptoms after obstetric or surgical injury in people.

Animal evidence

In the 2019 experiment, laser plus stem cells produced higher resting pressure than injury-only, laser-only, or stem-cell-only groups. Maximum squeeze pressure improved in all treated groups relative to the injured group, with no clear difference among treatments. The combination also increased selected muscle and vascular repair markers. These findings suggest that PBM contributed to a repair response, while several of the strongest results depended on adding cells rather than PBM alone (Sarveazad et al. 2019).

In the 2021 experiment, PBM alone, chondroitinase alone, and their combination improved resting pressure over sphincterotomy controls; the combination produced the highest resting pressure and improved tissue structure. The studies therefore show functional and tissue changes in rabbits, but they do not establish the added value of PBM for human continence (Sarveazad et al. 2021).

In-vitro and ex-vivo evidence

No standalone cell-culture or ex-vivo PBM study directly addressing this indication was identified. The stem cells in the 2019 paper were delivered as a co-treatment in the rabbit experiment, not studied as a separate PBM cell-culture programme.

Treatment Parameters and Generalizability

The 2019 study used 660-nm red visible laser light for 90 seconds immediately after injury and then daily for 14 days. The report described treatment alongside injection of two million human adipose-derived stem cells in relevant groups. Parameter reporting for the 2021 paper is incomplete in the database; it identifies 660-nm red light but does not give a sufficiently clear full dose schedule. Neither experiment compared wavelengths or doses.

Interpretation

The rabbit experiments report higher sphincter pressures and improved muscle or tissue markers, with combination treatments affecting some outcomes more than PBM alone. This is a useful proof of concept for repair after a defined surgical injury. The evidence remains very low for clinical use because the findings come from one research group, small animal groups, and no patient study.

Evidence strength in source summaryVery low for sphincter function after experimental injury in rabbits
Publications and records2 articles

Evidence strength rationale and next steps

Two small rabbit experiments found higher resting or squeeze pressures and changes in muscle and repair markers after PBM, particularly when combined with stem cells or chondroitinase. Both came from one research group and neither involved patients. Independent animal replication separating PBM from each added treatment, followed by carefully controlled clinical work, is needed before estimating a patient benefit.
